## Lecture material

### Start with a founder's question

Lectures 1 to 3 related an outcome to one predictor. Founders rarely think
about one factor at a time. Sales depend on the price, the advertising
budget, and the time of year together, and a founder wants to know how much
each of them matters on its own. Founders also want to compare like with
like. To judge a new website, for example, you would compare weeks in the
same season and with the same promotions, not any two weeks. Such events and
conditions enter the analysis as control variables. Multiple regression
describes how an outcome is related to several variables at the same time,
and how one relationship looks when the others are held fixed.

The Shark Tank file raises such a question. Founders who ask for more money
tend to offer slightly less equity. Offers also fell strongly over the
seasons: in the Lecture 3 practice, each later season went with about 0.82
percentage points less equity offered, about 6% of the mean offer of 13.2%.
If the requested amounts also changed over the seasons, the simple slope of
the requested amount could partly reflect the season trend. A founder who
wants to know what a larger request goes with should therefore compare
pitches from the same season. This lecture shows how to fit and read such a
model, when its coefficients differ from the simple slope, how to compare
models with different numbers of predictors, and what control variables can
and cannot tell you.

### More than one predictor

A model with one predictor compares cases that may differ in many other
ways. To hold a second factor fixed, put it into the model as well. For
predictors $X_{i1},\ldots,X_{ik}$, the model is

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kX_{ik}+\varepsilon_i,
$$

with conditional mean

$$
E[Y_i\mid X_{i1}=x_1,\ldots,X_{ik}=x_k]
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_kx_k.
$$

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Partial regression coefficient** (often called partial slope). The
coefficient $\beta_j$ of one predictor in a model with several predictors. It is the expected difference in $Y$ that goes with a
one-unit difference in $X_j$, holding the other included predictors fixed.

**Holding the other predictors fixed.** The comparison is between cases that
have the same values of all other predictors in the model and differ only in
$X_j$. Econometrics textbooks use the Latin term ceteris paribus, which
means "other things equal".
:::

Write the phrase "holding the other included predictors fixed" in every
interpretation of a slope from a multiple regression.

The model makes this comparison. The data do not need to contain two
real pitches that are the same in every other respect. The model compares
conditional means at fixed values of the included predictors.

### Why coefficients change: an invented example

Before answering the Shark Tank question, look at a case where the answer is
known. In an invented example we build the data ourselves, so we know the
true relationships. Imagine 180 small firms in three size classes: 60 small,
60 medium, and 60 large firms. The size of the firm (`size`, with the values
6, 10, and 14 in invented units) influences both advertising spend
(`adspend`) and revenue (`revenue`). Advertising itself adds nothing to revenue: the line of code
that builds `revenue` contains `size` but not `adspend`. The code builds the
three variables, then fits two models: revenue on advertising alone, and
revenue on advertising and size. It prints the coefficients of each.

```{r}
#| label: i04-sim-build
set.seed(42)
n <- 180
size    <- rep(c(6, 10, 14), each = n / 3)      # Z: firm size (drives both)
adspend <- 2 + 0.8 * size + rnorm(n, sd = 1)    # X: bigger firms spend more
revenue <- 5 + 1.5 * size + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)  # Y: size drives revenue,
demo <- data.frame(revenue, adspend, size)      #    adspend does not
coef(lm(revenue ~ adspend, data = demo))
coef(lm(revenue ~ adspend + size, data = demo))
```

The simple slope of `adspend` is about $1.66$: one more unit of advertising
goes with 1.66 more units of revenue, about 8% of the mean revenue of 20.
Yet we know that advertising does
nothing in these data. Once `size` is in the model, the slope of `adspend`
falls to about $-0.02$, close to the zero that we built in, and the slope of
`size` is about $1.52$, close to the 1.5 that we built in. One step up in
size class, 4 units, goes with about $4\times1.52\approx6.1$ more units of
revenue at the same advertising spend, about 30% of the mean revenue: a
large difference. The simple slope counted the effect of differences in size as an effect of
`adspend`. As a
description the simple slope is correct: firms that advertise more do have
higher revenue on average. As an answer to the question of what advertising
does, it is wrong.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Omitted variable.** A variable that is related to the outcome but is left
out of the model.

**Confounder.** An omitted variable that is related to both a predictor and
the outcome. The slope of that predictor then also picks up the relationship
between the confounder and the outcome. This distortion is the omitted
variable bias of Lecture 2. In the invented example, `size` is the confounder of
`adspend`.
:::

Why does the slope change so much? @fig-i04-ovb-scatter makes the two
comparisons visible. It plots revenue (vertical axis) against advertising
spend (horizontal axis) for the 180 invented firms. Each point is one firm,
and its colour and shape show its size class: blue circles for small firms,
green squares for medium firms, and orange triangles for large firms. The
figure contains two kinds of lines, built in different ways.

- The solid navy line is the simple regression line of revenue on
  advertising, fitted to all 180 firms at once. Its slope is the 1.66 of the
  first model.
- The three dashed lines come from the model with `size`. Its fitted
  equation is $\widehat{\text{revenue}}=4.98-0.02\,\text{adspend}+1.52\,
  \text{size}$. For each size class the code puts the size, 6, 10, or 14,
  into this equation. This gives one line per size class, drawn over the
  advertising spend of the firms in that class. All three lines have the
  same slope of $-0.02$. They lie about 6.1 units of revenue apart, the
  $4\times1.52$ for one step in size.

```{r}
#| label: fig-i04-ovb-scatter
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-cap: "Invented data: revenue against advertising spend for 180 simulated firms in three size classes. The solid line is the simple regression line. The dashed lines are the fitted lines of the model with size, one for each size class. The upward direction of the whole cloud comes from size alone. Within a size class the relationship is flat."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of revenue against advertising spend for 180 invented firms in three colours: small firms at the lower left, medium firms in the middle, large firms at the upper right. A solid line rises through the whole cloud. Three short dashed lines, one through each size group, are flat."
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)
n <- 180
size    <- rep(c(6, 10, 14), each = n / 3)      # Z: firm size (drives both)
adspend <- 2 + 0.8 * size + rnorm(n, sd = 1)    # X: bigger firms spend more
revenue <- 5 + 1.5 * size + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)  # Y: size drives revenue,
demo <- data.frame(revenue, adspend, size)      #    adspend does not
demo$group <- factor(demo$size, levels = c(6, 10, 14),
                     labels = c("Small firms (size 6)",
                                "Medium firms (size 10)",
                                "Large firms (size 14)"))
simple_fit <- lm(revenue ~ adspend, data = demo)
size_fit <- lm(revenue ~ adspend + size, data = demo)
# one fitted line of the model with size for each size class
within_lines <- data.frame(
  group = levels(demo$group),
  intercept = coef(size_fit)[1] + coef(size_fit)[3] * c(6, 10, 14),
  slope = coef(size_fit)[2],
  x_from = tapply(demo$adspend, demo$group, min),
  x_to = tapply(demo$adspend, demo$group, max)
)
within_lines$group <- factor(within_lines$group, levels = levels(demo$group))

ggplot(demo, aes(x = adspend, y = revenue,
                 colour = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(simple_fit)[1],
              slope = coef(simple_fit)[2],
              colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  geom_segment(data = within_lines,
               aes(x = x_from, xend = x_to,
                   y = intercept + slope * x_from,
                   yend = intercept + slope * x_to,
                   colour = group),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.3, y = 23, label = "simple regression line",
           hjust = 0, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.6) +
  annotate("segment", x = 6.6, y = 22.4, xend = 9.4,
           yend = coef(simple_fit)[1] + coef(simple_fit)[2] * 9.4 + 0.3,
           colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 0.5,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Small firms (size 6)" = "#0072B2",
    "Medium firms (size 10)" = "#009E73",
    "Large firms (size 14)" = "#D55E00"
  )) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    "Small firms (size 6)" = 16,
    "Medium firms (size 10)" = 15,
    "Large firms (size 14)" = 17
  )) +
  labs(x = "Advertising spend (invented units)",
       y = "Revenue (invented units)",
       colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )
```

Read the figure in two steps. First look at the whole cloud. Large firms
are high on both axes, and small firms are low on both. If you move from
left to right through the whole cloud, you move from small firms to large
firms, and revenue rises because size rises. The solid line follows this
movement, so the simple slope compares different kinds of firms. Then look
within one colour. The firms of one size class differ in advertising spend,
but their revenue does not rise with it: each group forms a flat cloud, and
its dashed line is flat. At a given size, more advertising does not go with
more revenue. The rise of the solid line comes from the jumps between the
three groups, not from the slope within any of them.

A coefficient changes when the added predictor explains differences that
the simple slope had picked up. This is why the phrase "holding the other
included predictors fixed" matters: it says which comparison the estimate
makes.

### The real-data contrast: the requested amount, with and without the season

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Now return to the question of the founder and
make the same comparison on the Shark Tank data. From here on, money is
measured in thousands of dollars: `ask_1k` is the requested amount divided
by 1,000. One unit is \$1,000 and 100 units are \$100,000. Lecture 1 showed
how a coefficient changes when the units of measurement change. The code
fits two models of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`, in percent) for
all 1,441 pitches: the simple model with the requested amount only
(`m_simple`), and the model that adds the season (`m_adjusted`). It prints
the coefficient table of each.

```{r}
#| label: i04-compare-slopes
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
m_simple   <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ ask_1k, data = sharks)
m_adjusted <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ ask_1k + season, data = sharks)
summary(m_simple)$coefficients
summary(m_adjusted)$coefficients
```

In the simple model the slope of `ask_1k` is about $-0.00329$, with
standard error $0.00063$: each additional \$1,000 requested goes with about
0.0033 percentage points less equity offered. With the season in the model
the slope is about $-0.00287$, with standard error $0.00058$. Holding the
season fixed, each additional \$1,000 requested goes with about 0.0029
percentage points less equity offered. The slope moves towards zero by about
13%. This answers the prediction question from before class: the
coefficient stays about the same, and the relationship between the
requested amount and the equity offered is largely stable when the season
is held fixed. The season itself has a slope of about $-0.814$ percentage
points per season, close to the simple season trend of Lecture 3.

Why does the slope move a little, and why not more? The correlation from the
warm-up between the season and the requested amount is only 0.04, so later
pitches asked for only slightly larger amounts. But the season is strongly
related to the equity offered. Pitches with large requests came a little
more often from later seasons, where offers were lower anyway, so the simple
slope picked up a small part of the season trend. Holding the season fixed
removes this part. In the invented example, `size` moved closely together
with advertising and removed the whole simple slope. Here the season hardly
moves together with the requested amount, so it removes only a small part.

The standard error of the slope also falls, from 0.00063 to 0.00058. The
season explains a large part of the differences in the equity offered that
the requested amount leaves unexplained, so the remaining noise around the
fitted values is smaller and the slope is estimated more precisely. The
section on control variables below returns to this.

Is the relationship large? The code below calculates the benchmarks of
Lecture 3: the mean and the standard deviation of the equity offered, the
standard deviation of `ask_1k`, the fitted change per \$100,000 in both
models, and the fitted change for a request one standard deviation higher in
the model with the season.

```{r}
#| label: i04-ask-magnitude
round(c(
  mean_equity = mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct),
  sd_equity = sd(sharks$equity_offered_pct),
  sd_ask_1k = sd(sharks$ask_1k),
  per_100k_simple = unname(100 * coef(m_simple)["ask_1k"]),
  per_100k_adjusted = unname(100 * coef(m_adjusted)["ask_1k"]),
  one_sd_adjusted = unname(sd(sharks$ask_1k) * coef(m_adjusted)["ask_1k"])
), 3)
```

The mean equity offered is 13.2% and its standard deviation is 8.4
percentage points. Per \$100,000 more requested, the equity offered is about
0.33 percentage points lower in the simple model and about 0.29 percentage
points lower at the same season. This is about 2.5% and 2.2% of the mean
offer. The
[Mathematics Refresher](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#numbers-proportions-percentages-and-units)
explains the difference between percentage points and percent. Typical
requests differ by much more than \$100,000: the standard deviation of the
requested amount is about 348.5 thousand dollars, about \$348,000. A request
one standard deviation higher goes with about 1.0 percentage point less
equity offered at the same season. This is about 8% of the mean offer and
0.12 standard deviations of the outcome. So the relationship is clearly
different from zero ($t\approx-5.0$), but small in business terms. This is
the lesson of
[Significant is not the same as large](i03-inference-fit-ftest.qmd#i03-significant-large)
in Lecture 3.

The stable slope is useful to know. The association between a larger
request and a smaller equity offer is not a by-product of the season trend,
because it also holds among pitches from the same season. As with every
model in this lecture, this statement covers the variables in the model.
The section on control variables below discusses what lies outside it.

### A three-predictor Shark Tank model

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A model can hold several factors fixed at
once. To practise reading such a model, add a third predictor that
describes the pitch itself. The outcome is the equity that the founders
offered at the start of the pitch (`equity_offered_pct`), in percent. The
predictors are:

- `season`, the season number, 1 to 16,
- `ask_1k`, the requested amount in thousands of dollars,
- `description_words`, the number of words in the short description of the
  business in the data source.

The description length is a rough measure of how much there is to say about
a business. A longer description may point to a more developed venture,
whose founders may offer less equity. The code fits the model and prints the
full summary, in the same layout as in Lecture 3.

```{r}
#| label: i04-fit
equity_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words,
  data = sharks
)
summary(equity_model)
```

The output has one row for each coefficient, with its estimate, standard
error, t statistic, and p-value. The column of estimates gives the fitted
equation, approximately

$$
\widehat{\text{equity}}
=22.025-0.836\,\text{season}-0.0029\,\text{ask\_1k}
-0.128\,\text{description\_words}.
$$

The bottom lines describe the whole model. The residual standard error of
7.6 percentage points is the typical distance between an actual and a fitted
offer, a little less than the standard deviation of the outcome (8.4). $R^2$
is 0.188, so the three predictors together account for about 19% of the
variation in the equity offered. The F statistic of 110.6 tests whether all
three slopes are zero at once, and its p-value is far below 0.05. The next
step is to read each slope.

#### The coefficient-interpretation protocol

A slope helps a reader only if the reader can tell what was compared, in
which units, and among which cases. Use the same five checks every time you
interpret a slope:

1. **Estimate and direction:** state the fitted change and its sign.
2. **Predictor step and unit:** say what a one-unit increase means.
3. **Outcome unit:** state the unit in which the outcome changes.
4. **Conditioning:** name the other included predictors that are held fixed.
5. **Scope:** name the analysed records and write "associated with", unless
   the data come from an experiment that justifies a causal claim.

The three predictors have different units:

| Term | A one-unit increase means | Coefficient unit |
|---|---|---|
| `season` | one later season | equity percentage points per season |
| `ask_1k` | \$1,000 more requested | equity percentage points per \$1,000 |
| `description_words` | one additional word | equity percentage points per word |

Apply the five checks to each slope in turn. All three sentences are about
the 1,441 recorded pitches:

- **Season.** At the same requested amount and description length, one later
  season is associated with about $0.836$ percentage points less equity
  offered. The t statistic of about $-16.4$ shows that the slope is clearly
  different from zero. It is also large: per season it is about 6% of the
  mean offer of 13.2%, and over five seasons it adds up to about 4.2
  percentage points, a third of the mean offer.
- **Requested amount.** At the same season and description length, an
  additional \$1,000 requested is associated with about $0.0029$ percentage
  points less equity offered. The number is tiny because the unit step is
  tiny. Per additional \$100,000 the association is about $0.29$ percentage
  points, about 2% of the mean offer: small, as in the model with the season
  only. The t statistic (about $-5.0$) does not depend on the unit.
- **Description length.** At the same season and requested amount, one
  additional description word is associated with about $0.128$ percentage
  points less equity offered, about 1% of the mean offer. This estimate is
  not statistically distinguishable from zero at 5% (p $\approx$ 0.26).
  Report the estimate anyway. "Not significant" does not mean "exactly
  zero". It means that the data are consistent with a range of values that
  includes zero. The section on size below shows which values this range
  still rules out.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check: the slope of the requested amount was −0.00329 alone, −0.00287 with the season, and −0.00290 with three predictors. Contradiction?

No. The three coefficients answer different questions. $-0.00329$ holds
nothing fixed. $-0.00287$ holds the season fixed. $-0.00290$ holds the
season and the description length fixed. Adding a predictor changes what is
held fixed, so the coefficient may change. Here all three changes are small,
because the requested amount moves together with neither the season nor
the description length.
:::

### Three models in one table {#i04-spec-table}

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A reader who wants to know whether a
coefficient changes when predictors are added needs all models at once, not
three separate outputs. This lecture has now fitted three models of the
equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`): the requested amount alone
(`m_simple`), the requested amount and the season (`m_adjusted`), and the
three-predictor model (`equity_model`). Research papers show such models
side by side in one table, with one column per model. The table needs the
estimate and standard error of every coefficient, which the outputs above
already show, and the fit of every model. The code below collects the number
of observations, $R^2$, and adjusted $R^2$ of the three models. Adjusted
$R^2$ is introduced in the next section.

```{r}
#| label: i04-spec-summaries
models <- list("(1)" = m_simple, "(2)" = m_adjusted, "(3)" = equity_model)
round(sapply(models, function(m) c(
  n = nobs(m),
  r_squared = summary(m)$r.squared,
  adj_r_squared = summary(m)$adj.r.squared
)), 4)
```

The table below collects these numbers and the coefficients from the
outputs above.

::: {.reg-table}
| | (1) | (2) | (3) |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Amount requested (\$1,000s) | −0.00329\*\*\* | −0.00287\*\*\* | −0.00290\*\*\* |
| | (0.00063) | (0.00058) | (0.00058) |
| Season | | −0.814\*\*\* | −0.836\*\*\* |
| | | (0.047) | (0.051) |
| Description length (words) | | | −0.128 |
| | | | (0.114) |
| Intercept | 14.139\*\*\* | 21.185\*\*\* | 22.025\*\*\* |
| | (0.284) | (0.483) | (0.888) |
| Observations | 1,441 | 1,441 | 1,441 |
| $R^2$ | 0.018 | 0.187 | 0.188 |
| Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.018 | 0.186 | 0.186 |
:::

Outcome: equity offered (%). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in
parentheses. All three columns use the same 1,441 pitches. The row of the
requested amount has more decimals because its unit step, \$1,000, is small.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.

Each column is one model and each row is one predictor. An empty space means
that the predictor is not in that model. The number in parentheses under a
coefficient is its standard error, and the stars show the p-value of the
two-sided test of that coefficient against zero. Read along a row to see how
a coefficient changes when predictors are added: the coefficient of the
requested amount moves from $-0.00329$ to $-0.00287$ when the season is
added, and stays at $-0.00290$ when the description length is added. Read
down a column to see one model: column (3) is `equity_model`. The bottom
rows give the number of observations and the fit of each model. This is the
layout to use for regression results in your thesis.

The fit rows tell a clear story. The requested amount alone explains less
than 2% of the variation in the equity offered ($R^2=0.018$). Adding the
season raises $R^2$ to 0.187, so the two predictors together explain about
19%. Adding the description length raises $R^2$ only from 0.1869 to 0.1876.
Is this last, tiny rise a real improvement? $R^2$ cannot answer this
question, and the next section shows why.

### Adjusted R²: comparing models with different numbers of predictors {#i04-adjusted-r2}

A founder who compares models wants to know whether an extra predictor
improves the model or only makes it more complicated. $R^2$ is a poor guide
for this choice, because it never falls when a predictor is added. Recall
from the Lecture 3 practice that adding a predictor cannot increase SSE:
least squares could always set the new slope to zero and keep the old fit.
Even a column of random numbers raises $R^2$ a little, because the fitted
model uses the chance patterns in that column to make SSE slightly smaller.
So a model with more predictors always looks at least as good by $R^2$,
whether or not the new predictors are useful.

Adjusted $R^2$ corrects for this. It compares SSE and SST after dividing each
by its degrees of freedom, so that every predictor has a price.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Adjusted $R^2$.** For a model with $k$ predictors and $n$ observations,

$$
R^2_{\text{adjusted}}
=1-\frac{\text{SSE}/(n-k-1)}{\text{SST}/(n-1)}
=1-(1-R^2)\,\frac{n-1}{n-k-1}.
$$

Written as $R^2$ minus a penalty, the same formula reads

$$
R^2_{\text{adjusted}}
=R^2-\underbrace{(1-R^2)\,\frac{k}{n-k-1}}_{\text{penalty}}.
$$

Use adjusted $R^2$ to compare models with different numbers of predictors,
fitted to the same outcome and the same observations.
:::

The penalty has three parts, and each has an intuitive meaning.

- The number of predictors $k$: every added predictor raises the penalty,
  so a new predictor must earn its place.
- The residual degrees of freedom $n-k-1$: with many observations per
  predictor the penalty is small, and with few observations it is large.
- The unexplained share $1-R^2$: the penalty is a share of the variation
  that the model still leaves unexplained.

Adding a predictor therefore has two opposite consequences. SSE falls, which
raises $R^2$, and $k$ rises, which raises the penalty. Adjusted $R^2$ rises
only when the new predictor lowers SSE by more than a predictor without any
relationship to the outcome would by chance. Otherwise it falls. When the
predictors add almost nothing, adjusted $R^2$ can even be negative.

::: {#exm-i04-adjusted-r2}
## Worked example: when more predictors lower adjusted R²

An invented model with $k=1$ predictor, fitted to $n=21$ weeks of sales,
has $R^2=0.50$. Its adjusted $R^2$ is

$$
0.50-(1-0.50)\,\frac{1}{21-1-1}=0.50-0.50\times\frac{1}{19}
=0.50-0.026=0.474.
$$

Adding four more predictors raises $R^2$ to 0.55. Now $k=5$ and

$$
0.55-(1-0.55)\,\frac{5}{21-5-1}=0.55-0.45\times\frac{5}{15}
=0.55-0.15=0.40.
$$

$R^2$ rose by 5 percentage points, but adjusted $R^2$ fell from 0.474 to
0.40. Four extra predictors explained too little to be worth their price
with only 21 observations.
:::

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} In the regression table the sample is large,
$n=1{,}441$, so the penalty is tiny. For model (3), with $k=3$, it is
$(1-0.1876)\times3/1437\approx0.0017$, so adjusted $R^2$ is $0.1876-0.0017
=0.1859$. Adding the season to the requested amount raises adjusted $R^2$
from 0.018 to 0.186: the season adds real explanatory power. Adding the
description length leaves adjusted $R^2$ practically unchanged at 0.186:
this predictor adds almost nothing to the fit.

The penalty matters most when there are many predictors for few
observations. The code below shows this. It takes 50 random pitches and
fits the model with the season and the requested amount. It then adds ten
columns of pure random numbers, which by construction have nothing to do
with the equity offered, and prints $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ of both models.

```{r}
#| label: i04-adjusted-r2-noise
set.seed(42)
small <- sharks[sample(nrow(sharks), 50),
                c("equity_offered_pct", "season", "ask_1k")]
for (j in 1:10) small[[paste0("noise", j)]] <- rnorm(50)
fit_two   <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = small)
fit_noise <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ ., data = small)
round(c(r2_two = summary(fit_two)$r.squared,
        adj_r2_two = summary(fit_two)$adj.r.squared,
        r2_noise = summary(fit_noise)$r.squared,
        adj_r2_noise = summary(fit_noise)$adj.r.squared), 3)
```

With the two real predictors, $R^2$ is 0.269 and adjusted $R^2$ is 0.237.
With the ten random columns added, $R^2$ rises to 0.378. Ten useless
predictors seem to explain 11 percentage points more of the variation, a
rise of 40%. Adjusted $R^2$ falls to 0.176. Its penalty for the twelve
predictors is $(1-0.378)\times12/(50-12-1)\approx0.20$, larger than the
apparent gain in $R^2$. So adjusted $R^2$ correctly shows that the random
columns add nothing real, while $R^2$ alone would suggest a better model.

### Scaling to comparisons readers care about

The table and adjusted $R^2$ help you choose a model. Once you have chosen
one, you report its coefficients to other people: the readers of your report
or thesis, an investor, or your own team. These readers rarely think in the
units of the table. An investor asks what a request of half a million
dollars more goes with, not one of \$1,000 more, and your team plans over
several seasons rather than one. So scale each coefficient to a step that
matters to these readers: fitted change = coefficient × number of unit
steps, holding the other included predictors fixed.

::: {#exm-i04-scaling}
## Worked example: five seasons, half a million dollars, two words

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Holding the other included predictors fixed in `equity_model`:

- **Five later seasons:** $5\times(-0.836)=-4.18$ fitted equity percentage
  points.
- **$500,000 more requested:** $500{,}000/1{,}000 = 500$ units of `ask_1k`,
  so $500\times(-0.0029)=-1.45$ fitted percentage points.
- **Two additional description words:** $2\times(-0.128)=-0.26$ fitted
  percentage points. The descriptions are short, and two words is about one
  standard deviation of their length, as the next section shows. This coefficient is
  not significantly different from zero, so the scaled version is not
  either.

Changing the units of measurement of a predictor changes the coefficient and
its standard error by the same factor. It does not change the fitted values, the t
statistic, or the relationship itself. A coefficient "per dollar" of
$-0.0000029$ would be correct but hard to read. Per \$1,000 is readable. Per
\$100,000 is often the best unit for a sentence.
:::

### Significant is not the same as large

Scaling gives the change in readable units. Whether that change is large is
a separate question. Lecture 3 showed that a small p-value does not make a
coefficient large, and that a result without stars can still be informative
([Significant is not the same as large](i03-inference-fit-ftest.qmd#i03-significant-large)).
The same holds in a model with several predictors. The code below
calculates the benchmarks for `equity_model`: the fitted change for five
seasons and for a request one standard deviation higher, the mean and the
standard deviation of the description length, and the 95% interval of the
description slope for a step of one standard deviation.

```{r}
#| label: i04-size-benchmarks
b <- coef(equity_model)
ci_words <- confint(equity_model)["description_words", ]
round(c(
  five_seasons = unname(5 * b["season"]),
  one_sd_ask = unname(sd(sharks$ask_1k) * b["ask_1k"]),
  mean_words = mean(sharks$description_words),
  sd_words = sd(sharks$description_words),
  ci_one_sd_words = ci_words * sd(sharks$description_words)
), 3)
```

With the mean equity offered of 13.2% and its standard deviation of 8.4
percentage points as benchmarks:

- five later seasons go with 4.18 fewer percentage points, 32% of the mean
  offer and half a standard deviation of the outcome, a large difference,
- a request one standard deviation higher, about \$348,000, goes with 1.01
  fewer percentage points, 8% of the mean and 0.12 standard deviations, a
  small difference although the coefficient has three stars,
- the description length has no stars, but its interval is still
  informative: the descriptions have a mean of 5 words, and for a step of
  one standard deviation, about 1.9 words, the 95% interval runs from
  $-0.67$ to $0.18$ percentage points, so the data rule out an association
  larger than about 5% of the mean offer for typical differences in
  description length.

Report the size next to the significance every time.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Try it: three seasons later and $200,000 more

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Two pitches have the same description
length. One is three seasons later and requests $200,000 more. Complete the
steps before opening the answer.

*Step 1 (given).* Three seasons contribute $3\times(-0.836)$ fitted
percentage points.

*Step 2 (you).* Convert $200,000 into `ask_1k` units (thousands of
dollars). Multiply by the `ask_1k` coefficient, about $-0.0029$ percentage
points per \$1,000.

*Step 3 (you).* Add the two contributions. This is allowed because the model
is additive: each predictor has its own term, and the terms are added up.
State the combined fitted difference in one sentence that passes the five
checks of the coefficient-interpretation protocol.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

$200{,}000/1{,}000=200$ units, so the request contributes
$200\times(-0.0029)\approx-0.58$. Combined:
$3(-0.836)+200(-0.0029)\approx-2.51-0.58=-3.09$ percentage points. Sentence:
among the recorded pitches, a pitch three seasons later that requests
\$200,000 more is fitted to offer about 3.1 percentage points less equity,
holding description length fixed.

```{r}
#| label: i04-faded-check
b <- coef(equity_model)
3 * b["season"] + 200 * b["ask_1k"]
```
:::
:::

### What control variables can and cannot do

The Shark Tank models added the season to check the relationship between
the requested amount and the equity offered, and the invented example added
firm size. Before you add variables to your
own models, it helps to know what this step can achieve. A control variable
(often just called a control) is a predictor that is included in the model
so that the comparison holds it fixed. Including a control variable can

- make a comparison fairer, because the compared cases are alike on the
  measured variables,
- reduce the residual variation, which makes confidence intervals narrower,
  as the season did for the slope of the requested amount,
- show that a simple association partly came from comparing different kinds
  of cases.

A control variable also has a cost when it moves closely together with the
predictor that you are interested in. Take the invented example of firm size
and advertising. With `size` in the model, the advertising slope compares
firms of the same size. But firms of the same size differ only a little in
advertising spend. In @fig-i04-ovb-scatter, the points of one colour cover a
much narrower range of advertising spend than all points together. With so
little variation in advertising, the data say less about its slope. Its
standard error grows, and its confidence interval gets wider. The code
below prints the correlation between advertising spend and size, the
standard deviation of advertising spend among all firms and within each size
class, and then the advertising slope and its standard error, first without
and then with `size` in the model.

```{r}
#| label: i04-precision-cost
round(cor(demo$adspend, demo$size), 2)
# spread of adspend among all firms and within each size class
round(c(all_firms = sd(demo$adspend),
        tapply(demo$adspend, demo$size, sd)), 2)
# slope of adspend and its standard error, without and with size
round(summary(lm(revenue ~ adspend, data = demo))$coefficients["adspend", 1:2], 3)
round(summary(lm(revenue ~ adspend + size, data = demo))$coefficients["adspend", 1:2], 3)
```

Advertising spend and size have a correlation of about 0.93, close to the
maximum of 1. Among all firms, advertising spend has a standard deviation of
about 2.8. Within a size class it is only between about 0.9 and 1.15, roughly a third of that.
The standard error of the advertising slope is about 0.06 without `size` and
about 0.11 with `size` in the model, almost twice as large. Here the control
is still needed, because without it the slope mixes advertising with size.
But the estimate that you get is less precise. The section on
multicollinearity below explains this cost and what to do about it.

Including a control variable cannot

- adjust for variables that were not measured,
- fix reverse causality, where the outcome influences the predictor,
- repair selection, where the cases in the file are not typical of the
  cases you want to talk about,
- remove errors in how a variable was measured.

A control variable is simply a predictor like any other. The word
"control" does not make any coefficient causal. Only the way the data
were produced can make a coefficient causal, for example when the data come
from an experiment.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check: which of these four problems does adding `season` address?

&#40;a) Pitches with large requests come slightly more often from later
seasons, when offers were lower anyway. (b) The experience of the founder is
not recorded. (c) The equity offered may influence how much is asked. (d)
Only pitches that were broadcast are in the file.

Only (a). The season is measured, and holding `season` fixed removes the
season trend from the comparison of requested amounts. Problem (b) is an
unmeasured confounder, (c) is reverse causality, and (d) is selection.
Adding a measured control variable does not solve any of these three.
:::

### Assumptions extend to the full predictor set

The standard errors, t statistics, and intervals in the table above are only
reliable if the model assumptions hold. For multiple regression, the
assumptions of Lecture 2 apply to the whole set of included predictors, and
one new assumption is added in the last row of the table below.

| Assumption | What it says with several predictors | How to check it | What goes wrong if it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linearity | The average of $Y$ is linear in the included terms: $E[Y\mid X_1,\ldots,X_k]=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\cdots+\beta_kX_k$ | Plot the residuals against the fitted values and against each predictor. Points spread evenly around zero agree with the assumption, a curve does not | The slopes miss part of the pattern, and the fitted values are wrong in some parts of the range |
| Homoskedasticity (constant variance) | The errors have the same variance at all values of the predictors | Residuals against fitted values. A band of equal width agrees with the assumption, a spread that grows or shrinks along the horizontal axis does not | The slopes stay unbiased, but the usual standard errors, tests, and intervals are wrong |
| Normality of the errors | The errors follow a normal distribution | A normal Q--Q plot of the residuals. Points close to the straight line agree with the assumption | In small samples the t and F distributions are no longer exact. In large samples this matters little |
| Independence (random sampling) | The error of one row says nothing about the error of another row | Knowledge of how the data were collected | The usual standard errors are often too small |
| Zero conditional mean (exogeneity): no omitted confounder | The error averages zero at all values of the included predictors | Knowledge of how the predictors came about. No plot can show it | A slope is not the effect of changing its predictor. It still describes how average outcomes differ, holding the other included predictors fixed |
| No perfect multicollinearity (new) | No predictor can be calculated exactly from the others, for example as the sum of two of them | R reports `NA` for a coefficient and leaves the term out. For high but not perfect correlations, look at the correlations among the predictors with `cor()` | With perfect multicollinearity a coefficient cannot be estimated at all. With high correlations the single slopes are imprecise |

The last assumption is new because it can only fail when a model has more
than one predictor. It needs two related terms.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Multicollinearity.** A high correlation among the predictors. It does not
bias the coefficients. It makes the single coefficients imprecise and
unstable, because the data contain little information to separate
predictors that move together.

**Perfect multicollinearity.** One predictor can be calculated exactly from
the others. Then one coefficient cannot be estimated at all, and R leaves
one term out of the model.
:::

The invented example showed multicollinearity at work: with a correlation of
0.93 between advertising and size, the standard error of the advertising
slope almost doubled, from about 0.06 to about 0.11. Why does this happen?
With `size` in the model, the advertising slope is estimated only from
comparisons between firms of the same size that differ in advertising. When
two predictors move together this closely, the data contain few such cases.
A firm with high advertising spend is almost always a large firm, so firms
whose advertising changes while their size stays fixed are rare. In the
invented data, advertising spend varies about three times less within a
size class than among all firms. The separate slope of advertising therefore
rests on little information, and little information means a large standard
error and a wide interval. The model still estimates both slopes without
bias. The data simply cannot tell the two predictors apart very well.

Multicollinearity does not harm prediction: the fitted values of the model
stay just as accurate. It matters when you want to read single slopes. In
practice, you can

- look at the correlations among the predictors with `cor()` before you
  read single slopes, and treat very high correlations, such as 0.9 or
  more, as a warning,
- keep a control variable that is a confounder even though it widens the
  interval, because dropping `size` here would give a precise but
  misleading slope of 1.66 instead of a slope close to zero,
- keep only one of two predictors, or combine them, when both measure the
  same thing, for example two measures of firm size,
- collect more data, ideally including cases in which the two predictors
  move apart, such as large firms with little advertising,
- report the wide interval openly, and test the two predictors together
  with the joint test of Lecture 5, which can show that they matter jointly
  even when neither slope is precise on its own.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} For the three-predictor Shark Tank model, the
code below prints the correlations among the three predictors.

```{r}
#| label: i04-predictor-correlations
round(cor(sharks[, c("season", "ask_1k", "description_words")]), 2)
```

Each number is the correlation between the predictors of its row and its
column, and the diagonal shows that each predictor has a correlation of 1
with itself. All correlations are small. The strongest is between the season
and the description length, at $-0.38$: later seasons have slightly shorter
descriptions. This is far from 0.9, so multicollinearity is not a concern in
this model.

### A coefficient plot keeps units visible

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A table gives exact numbers, but readers
often want to see at a glance which estimates are clearly different from
zero. A coefficient plot shows this. @fig-i04-coefplot shows the three slope
estimates of `equity_model` with their 95% confidence intervals. The code
takes the estimates and intervals from the model, rescales the requested
amount to steps of \$100,000, and draws one row per predictor.

```{r}
#| label: fig-i04-coefplot
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-cap: "Coefficient estimates from the three-predictor model of the equity offered, with 95% confidence intervals. Each row uses its own predictor unit: per season, per $100,000 requested, and per word. The sizes cannot be compared across rows without these units."
#| fig-alt: "Coefficient plot with three rows and a dashed vertical line at zero. Season: a dot at about minus 0.84 with a short interval well left of zero. Amount requested per 100,000 dollars: a dot at about minus 0.29 with a short interval left of zero. Description length per word: a dot at about minus 0.13 with a wide interval from about minus 0.35 to plus 0.09 that crosses zero."
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
equity_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words,
  data = sharks
)
ci <- confint(equity_model)[-1, , drop = FALSE]
# Show the requested amount per $100,000 instead of per $1,000 (x 100),
# so that its estimate and interval are visible on the same axis
unit_factor <- c(1, 100, 1)
term_labels <- c("Season (per season)", "Amount requested (per $100,000)",
                 "Description length (per word)")
coef_df <- data.frame(
  term = factor(term_labels, levels = term_labels),
  estimate = coef(equity_model)[-1] * unit_factor,
  lower = ci[, 1] * unit_factor,
  upper = ci[, 2] * unit_factor
)

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#C98B2E",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper),
                  colour = "#009E73", linewidth = 0.7, fatten = 2.6) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.02, y = 3.35, label = "no change = 0",
           hjust = 1, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  labs(x = "Estimated change in equity offered (percentage points)",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )
```

Read @fig-i04-coefplot with the
[five steps for reading a figure](../basic/b01-introduction-data-analysis.qmd#b01-read-graph):

1. **Unit and variables:** the rows are the predictors. The horizontal axis
   is the estimated change in the equity offered, in percentage points.
2. **Scales:** each estimate is per one unit of its own predictor: per
   season, per \$100,000 requested, per word. The rows are not on a common
   scale. The model uses `ask_1k`, in \$1,000s, so its coefficient is about
   $-0.0029$. Per \$1,000 that change is so small that its dot and interval
   would sit on the zero line. The plot therefore shows it per \$100,000:
   $100\times(-0.0029)\approx-0.29$ percentage points.
3. **One element:** a dot is a coefficient estimate, and its horizontal line
   is the 95% confidence interval. The dashed line marks zero.
4. **Pattern:** the intervals for the season and for the requested amount
   lie clearly left of zero. The interval for the description length
   crosses zero. The distance from zero in this plot depends on the unit
   that you choose. It does not show how strong the evidence is: for that,
   look at the t statistic or at whether the interval contains zero.
5. **Limits:** the intervals show sampling uncertainty under the model,
   among these recorded pitches.

::: {.caveat-box}
<span class="label">What an adjusted coefficient can and cannot say</span>

- "Holding fixed" covers only the predictors in the model. The maturity of
  the venture, its revenue, and the experience of the founder are not held
  fixed.
- If a coefficient stays stable across models, the measured control
  variables do not explain it. This proves nothing about variables that were not
  measured.
- The equity offered is the opening offer in the pitch, not a completed
  investment.

**What you can do with it:** add the control variables that a critic would name first.
If your coefficient stays about the same after you add them, you can act on it
for cheap decisions. For expensive decisions, test it first.
:::

### Answering the driving question

Yes, the relationship between the requested amount and the equity offered
is largely stable when you compare pitches from the same season. Without
the season, each additional \$100,000 requested goes with about 0.33
percentage points less equity offered. At the same season it is about 0.29
percentage points, a change of about 13%, and with the description length
also held fixed it stays at 0.29. The season hardly moved together with the
requested amount (correlation 0.04), so the season trend explained only a
small part of the simple slope, even though the trend itself is large:
about 0.8 percentage points per season. The relationship is clearly
different from zero ($t\approx-5.0$), but it is small in business terms:
about 2% of the mean offer of 13.2% per \$100,000, and about 1 percentage
point for a request one standard deviation, about \$348,000, higher.

As a founder deciding how much money to ask for, you might expect that
asking for \$500,000 more goes with an opening offer about 1.4 percentage
points lower than that of other founders in the same season
($500\times0.00287\approx1.4$), under the assumption that the recorded
pitches are typical of pitches like yours. The season matters much more:
five seasons go with about 4.2 percentage points less equity offered. So
when you set your own opening offer, compare it with recent pitches rather
than with the average over all seasons.

::: {.founder-box}
<span class="label">A founder's decision (invented example)</span>

You run a campus venture that sells meal boxes. In weeks with lower prices
you get more orders: the simple slope is 60 more orders per euro of price
cut. But you lowered prices mainly in exam weeks, when demand is high anyway.
With exam weeks in the model as a control variable, the slope is 25 orders
per euro. You sell about 150 meal boxes a week at a margin of 4 euros per
box. Should you cut the price by 1 euro?

Try it yourself first.

1. Which of the two slopes describes what a price cut does, and why?
2. How much margin does the cut cost you on the 150 boxes that you would sell
   anyway?
3. After the cut, each extra order earns 3 euros. How much margin do the
   extra orders bring, with each of the two slopes?
4. Decide.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## See the solution

1. The slope with the control variable, 25 orders per euro. The simple
   slope also counts the higher demand in exam weeks as an effect of the
   price.
2. $150\times1=150$ euros per week.
3. With the simple slope: $60\times3=180$ euros. With the adjusted slope:
   $25\times3=75$ euros.
4. With the simple slope the cut would look profitable, because 180 is more
   than 150. With the adjusted slope it is not, because 75 is less than 150.
   The decision: keep the price. The control variable changed the decision.
:::
:::

This lecture gave you multiple regression: one coefficient per predictor,
read while the other included predictors are held fixed, a regression table
to see how a coefficient changes when control variables are added, and
adjusted $R^2$ to compare models of different size. All predictors so far
were numbers, such as the season or the requested amount. Many questions
that founders ask are about groups instead. Does an online shop sell more
than a market stall? Did the customers who saw a new website version buy
more than those who saw the old one? Do teams of women open their pitch
with different equity offers from teams of men or mixed teams? Such categories cannot enter
a model as ordinary numbers. Lecture 5 shows how they enter a regression,
how to read the result of an A/B test as a regression, and how to test
whether a whole set of terms matters at once.

**Next:** Lecture 5 adds categories as predictors and introduces the joint
test of several coefficients.

:::

## After class

After the lecture, work through all the practice below.

### Read the lecture material

Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture
covered the main ideas. The text has every step, every example, and all the
code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still
unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly, the course AI
assistant.

### Recall questions

1. Which phrase belongs in every interpretation of a slope from a multiple
   regression?
2. Why can a coefficient change after another predictor is added?
3. What does the zero conditional mean condition (no omitted confounder) say, and when is it needed?
4. Why does adding control variables not make a coefficient causal?
5. What problem can strongly correlated predictors create?
6. Which five elements belong in the interpretation of a slope?
7. Why can adjusted $R^2$ fall when a predictor is added, while $R^2$
   cannot?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

1. "Holding the other included predictors fixed."
2. The simple slope also picks up the relationship between the outcome and an
   omitted variable that is related to the predictor. When that variable is
   added, the slope no longer includes this part.
3. The error averages zero at every value of the predictors: nothing outside
   the model drives both an included predictor and the outcome. It is needed only when a coefficient is read as the effect of
   changing that predictor.
4. Unmeasured confounders, selection, reverse causality, and measurement
   error can all remain after a control variable is added.
5. Imprecise and unstable estimates of the single coefficients. With perfect
   multicollinearity R cannot estimate all coefficients and leaves one term out.
6. Estimate and direction, predictor step and unit, outcome unit, the
   predictors that are held fixed, and the scope (which records, association
   or effect).
7. Adding a predictor cannot increase SSE, so $R^2$ cannot fall. Adjusted
   $R^2$ subtracts the penalty $(1-R^2)\,k/(n-k-1)$, which grows with every
   added predictor. If the new predictor lowers SSE by less than the
   penalty grows, adjusted $R^2$ falls.
:::

### Finish a half-worked example: interpret the two-predictor model

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Take the two-predictor model `m_adjusted`,
column (2) of the regression table. It regresses the equity offered by the
founder, in percent, on the season and the requested amount in thousands of
dollars (`ask_1k`), using all 1,441 pitches. Its fitted slopes are $-0.814$
per season and $-0.0029$ per \$1,000 requested. The mean equity offered is
13.2%. Interpret both slopes with units and with the predictor that is held
fixed, and judge the size of the requested-amount slope per \$100,000.

Step 1 (given). Season: holding the requested amount fixed, among the
recorded pitches, one later season is associated with about 0.814 percentage
points less equity offered. This is 6% of the mean offer per season.

Step 2 (you). Write the same kind of sentence for `ask_1k`, per \$100,000,
and compare the result with the mean offer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

Holding the season fixed, among the recorded pitches, an additional
\$100,000 requested is associated with about 0.29 percentage points less
equity offered ($100\times(-0.0029)$). This is about 2% of the mean offer of
13.2%, a small difference, although the coefficient is clearly different
from zero (t $\approx-5.0$).
:::

### Practice

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} All items use the three-predictor model `equity_model`. It regresses the equity offered by
the founder, in percent, on the season, the requested amount in thousands of
dollars (`ask_1k`), and the number of words in the description
(`description_words`), using all 1,441 pitches. The mean equity offered is
13.2% and its standard deviation is 8.4 percentage points.

1. Calculate 95% confidence intervals with `confint(equity_model)`.
2. Test each coefficient against zero. Explain how these three single tests
   differ from the one overall F-test of the model.
3. Remove `ask_1k`. Compare the coefficients of season and description
   length with those of the three-predictor model.
4. Name one plausible omitted variable and explain which interpretation of
   the coefficients it would make questionable.
5. Interpret a difference of eight seasons with the fitted season
   coefficient. Judge its size with the mean of the outcome.
6. Interpret a difference of \$250,000 in the requested amount. Judge its
   size with the mean of the outcome.
7. Interpret a difference of 3 words in description length, use the 95%
   interval to judge $H_0:\beta=0$, and judge which sizes the interval
   still rules out.
8. Compare two fitted pitches that are the same except that one is two
   seasons earlier and requests \$1,000,000 more. Calculate the combined
   fitted difference.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

1. The season interval is approximately $(-0.936, -0.736)$, the `ask_1k`
   interval $(-0.0040, -0.0018)$, and the description interval
   $(-0.351, 0.095)$.
2. Each t-test evaluates one $\beta_j=0$ at a time. The overall F-test
   (F $\approx$ 110.6 on 3 and 1437 df) evaluates all three slope
   coefficients together.
3. Without `ask_1k`, the season coefficient is about $-0.842$ (against
   $-0.836$) and the description coefficient about $-0.106$ (against
   $-0.128$, still not significant, p $\approx$ 0.36). The coefficients
   change only slightly, because the requested amount is hardly correlated
   with the season or with the description length.
4. Examples are the maturity of the venture, its revenue, the experience of
   the founder, or decisions of the producers about what is broadcast. If
   such a variable is related to both an included predictor and the equity
   offered, it is a confounder. The coefficient is then still a correct
   description, but it is not the effect of the predictor.
5. Holding requested amount and description length fixed, a pitch eight
   seasons later is fitted to offer $8\times(-0.836)\approx-6.69$ equity
   percentage points less. This is about half of the mean offer of 13.2%, a
   large difference.
6. \$250,000 equals 250 units of `ask_1k`. Holding season and description
   length fixed, the fitted difference is $250\times(-0.0029)\approx-0.72$
   percentage points. This is about 5% of the mean offer, a small
   difference.
7. 3 words go with about $3\times(-0.128)\approx-0.38$ fitted percentage
   points, holding season and requested amount fixed. Multiplying the
   interval by 3 gives approximately $(-1.05, 0.28)$. The interval contains
   zero, so the two-sided 5% test does not reject a zero coefficient. The
   interval rules out associations larger than about 1 percentage point in
   either direction, about 8% of the mean offer.
8. Two seasons earlier is $-2$ seasons, and \$1,000,000 is 1,000 units of
   `ask_1k`. The fitted difference is
   $-2\times(-0.836)+1000\times(-0.0029)\approx1.67-2.90=-1.23$ percentage
   points, holding description length fixed. The two contributions add
   because the model is additive, and here they partly cancel.
:::

### Practice: all steps together

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Write one paragraph that connects the diagnostics of Lecture 2 to
the three-predictor model of this lecture (`equity_model`): the equity
offered regressed on the season, the requested amount, and the description
length, for all 1,441 pitches. Which residual checks would you run on this three-predictor
model? What would each check look for? What would you do about a highly
influential pitch if you found one?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check a model answer

A plot of residuals against fitted values checks that the conditional mean
is roughly linear in the included terms and that the spread is roughly
constant. A curve would suggest that assumption 1 fails. A funnel, with a spread that grows or shrinks
along the fitted values, would suggest heteroskedasticity, and then the usual standard errors are wrong. Standardised residuals (`rstandard`)
flag pitches that the model fits unusually badly. Cook's distance flags
pitches that move the coefficients on their own. Investigate a flagged
pitch, for example one with an extreme requested amount, but do not delete
it. Check the recorded values, fit the model with and without it, and report
both fits if they disagree. Never delete an observation without reporting
it.
:::

### Review questions from past lectures

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Lecture 3 regressed the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on
the season alone, using all 1,441 pitches. In this simple model the slope's
t statistic is about $-17.34$. What is the overall F statistic of this one-predictor
model, and why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

$F = t^2 \approx 300.7$. With a single slope, the overall F-test and the
two-sided t-test of that slope test the same hypothesis, and F is exactly the
square of t. With several predictors this is no longer true. So Lecture 5
introduces a test of several coefficients at once.
:::

### Worked exam interpretation

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Exam-style question.** A summary table reports, for the model of the
equity offered on the season, the requested amount, and the description
length,
`season  -0.836  (SE 0.051)` and `description_words  -0.128  (SE 0.114)`. A
student writes: "Season matters and word count does not, so descriptions have
no effect on equity." Give two corrections.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check a model answer

First, "no effect" is a wrong reading of a result that is not significant. The interval
$(-0.351, 0.095)$ contains zero and also values near $-0.35$. The data are
consistent with no association and also with a small negative one. Not significant does
not mean zero. Second, "effect" claims causation. Both estimates are
associations among the recorded pitches, holding the other included
predictors fixed. The data do not come from an experiment, so they do not
show a causal effect.
:::

### Check the AI

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} You regressed the equity offered on the requested amount and the season. You asked an AI assistant: "I added the season as a control. Is the coefficient of the requested amount, -0.0029 per \$1,000, now the effect of asking for more money?" It answered:

> "Yes. Because you controlled for the season, asking for \$100,000 more now causes 0.29 percentage points less equity."

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the **Verify**
step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

A control variable only holds fixed what was measured and included. Venture maturity, founder experience, and the choices of the producers are not in the model, and they may be related to both the requested amount and the equity offered. The correct sentence: in the same season, an additional \$100,000 requested is associated with about 0.29 percentage points less equity offered, about 2% of the mean offer of 13.2%.
:::

### Make it yours

:::: {.utility-prompt}
<span class="label">Two sentences about your own venture</span>

Think of your own venture, or any business you know well. Name one
outcome you care about and two factors that influence it and are correlated
with each other (for example price and quality tier, or marketing spend and
firm age). Then write two sentences. What would a regression of the outcome
on only one of the two factors mix together? What would "holding the other
factor fixed" let you see? There is no wrong answer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## See an example, then write your own

Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus. "Outcome: weekly orders. Factors: price and quality tier, which move together because premium boxes cost more. A regression of orders on price alone would mix cheaper boxes with lower-tier boxes. Holding the tier fixed shows what a price cut does within a tier, and that is the number I can act on."
:::

You can discuss this task, and any other task in this chapter, with
Tilly for QM Intermediate, the course AI assistant. Ask it to propose an omitted variable for
the regression of your venture, and to ask you whether a measured control
variable could fix it.
